name: Qwen2.5-Coder 0.5B
desc: General tiny coder with no house style baked in. The Chromebook target — runs on ~4GB RAM, offline. The base model this project fine-tunes.
about:
The smallest member of Alibaba's Qwen2.5-Coder line, a family trained specifically for programming rather than general chat, then instruction-tuned so it answers requests instead of just continuing text.

This is the base model the Rules-Baker pipeline fine-tunes. It's the Chromebook target: small enough to sit in a 4GB machine's memory alongside the browser, and quick enough that a short function comes back in seconds. It knows Python syntax well; it does not reliably keep track of state across a long snippet, which is what the sandbox check is for.

name: Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B
desc: Larger tiny coder — noticeably smarter than the 0.5B, but needs ~3GB free RAM and is slower on a CPU. For laptops rather than Chromebooks.
about:
The same Qwen2.5-Coder family as the 0.5B, roughly three times the parameters.

Noticeably better at holding a whole function together — fewer undefined names, fewer half-finished blocks. The cost is memory and speed: it needs meaningfully more free RAM and generates slower on a CPU, which is why it's marked for laptops rather than Chromebooks.

name: Gemma 3 270M
desc: Google's smallest instruction-tuned model — a different family and tokenizer to Qwen, so a good side-by-side comparison. Smaller than the Chromebook default and loads fast, but it is a general chat model, not a coder.
about:
Google's smallest Gemma 3 release, instruction-tuned. A different lineage from Qwen entirely — different training data, different tokenizer, different architecture — which makes it the most useful comparison in this list.

It is a general chat model, not a coder. Expect weaker Python than Qwen2.5-Coder at a similar size, and expect it to be better at answering a plain question. Its value here is showing that the runtime is model-agnostic: same page, same sandbox, completely different weights.

name: Gemma 2 2B
desc: The strongest model here, and the largest that comfortably fits the browser's 4GB WASM limit. Laptop only — too big for a 4GB Chromebook.
about:
The previous Gemma generation at 2B parameters — the largest model in this library, and about the biggest that fits comfortably in the browser's 4GB WebAssembly address space.

The strongest general model here, but slow enough on CPU-only WebAssembly that you will feel every token. This is the one most worth running through Ollama instead, where it can use the GPU.

name: Llama 3.2 1B
desc: Meta's small instruct model. Third family in the list — same runtime, different weights, different training data. Chromebook-sized at Q4.
about:
Meta's small instruction-tuned Llama, and the third distinct family in the library.

Sits between the tiny models and Gemma 2 2B in both size and capability. General-purpose rather than code-specialised, so treat its Python as a starting point rather than an answer — the sandbox check matters more here than with the Qwen coders.

name: SmolLM2 135M
desc: Featherweight — the smallest, fastest model here. Weak, but loads in seconds. Best for testing that the in-browser runtime works on very low-end hardware.
about:
Hugging Face's own small-model family, built for running on devices rather than in a data centre. At 135M parameters it is the smallest thing here by a wide margin.

It is not going to write useful software. Its job in this project is proving the runtime works: it downloads in seconds on almost any connection and loads on hardware that cannot hold anything larger, so if the browser can run a model at all, it can run this one.

name: Smoke-test bake (yours)
desc: The first model baked with this project's pipeline, from mock data. It regurgitates a memorized house-style template regardless of the request — real proof the pipeline works, but not smart.
about:
Your own model — the first artefact produced by this project's Rules-Baker pipeline.

A LoRA adapter trained on a small mock dataset, merged back into Qwen2.5-Coder 0.5B and exported to GGUF. It overfits that mock data and will reproduce a memorised house-style template more or less regardless of what you ask, so it is not a useful assistant.

That is the point: it proves the whole loop — generate data, train, merge, quantise, run in the browser — works end to end. Real task-following behaviour needs a genuine teacher-generated dataset, which is the next stage.
